# Native gates and connectivity {#sec-native-gates}

{{< include _macros.qmd >}}

A circuit as written in an SDK is not what runs on a device. The hardware implements a
small set of [native gates]{.gloss key="native-gate"}, each a calibrated control pulse,
and only between the pairs of qubits that are physically coupled. This section builds the
one identity we need to read native gate sets, and then looks at what connectivity costs.

## Pauli rotations {#sec-pauli-rotations}

::: {#def-pauli-string}
## Pauli string
A [Pauli string]{.gloss key="pauli-string"} on $n$ qubits is a tensor product
$P = P_1 \otimes P_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes P_n$ with each $P_j \in \{I, X, Y, Z\}$.
We often drop the tensor product signs and write, for example, $ZZ$ or $XIY$.
:::

Every Pauli string is Hermitian and squares to the identity, $P^2 = I$, because each
single-qubit factor does. This one property is all we need for the following identity.

::: {#prp-pauli-rotation}
## Pauli rotations
Let $P$ be a Hermitian operator with $P^2 = I$, for example a Pauli string. Then for all
real $\theta$
$$
e^{-i\theta P/2} = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\, I - i \sin\frac{\theta}{2}\, P .
$$ {#eq-pauli-rotation}
:::

::: {.proof}
Expand the exponential as a power series. Since $P^2 = I$, even powers give
$P^{2m} = I$ and odd powers give $P^{2m+1} = P$, so
$$
e^{-i\theta P/2}
= \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^m}{(2m)!}\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)^{2m} I
\;-\; i \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^m}{(2m+1)!}\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)^{2m+1} P ,
$$
and the two series are those of $\cos(\theta/2)$ and $\sin(\theta/2)$.
:::

::: {#exm-rotations}
## Single- and two-qubit rotations
Applying @eq-pauli-rotation with $P = X$, $Z$ and $Z \otimes Z$ gives
$$
R_X(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\frac{\theta}{2} & -i\sin\frac{\theta}{2} \\
-i\sin\frac{\theta}{2} & \cos\frac{\theta}{2} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
R_Z(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix} e^{-i\theta/2} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{i\theta/2} \end{pmatrix},
$$ {#eq-rx-rz}
$$
R_{ZZ}(\theta) = e^{-i\theta Z\otimes Z/2}
= \operatorname{diag}\!\left(e^{-i\theta/2}, e^{i\theta/2}, e^{i\theta/2}, e^{-i\theta/2}\right).
$$ {#eq-rzz}
$R_{ZZ}$ applies a phase that depends only on the parity of the two bits. That is why it
can be built from two CNOTs and a single $R_Z$ (@fig-rzz): the first CNOT writes the
parity $a \oplus b$ into the second qubit, $R_Z$ applies the phase, and the second CNOT
undoes the first.
:::

![The decomposition $R_{ZZ}(\theta) = \gate{CNOT}\,(I \otimes R_Z(\theta))\,\gate{CNOT}$, drawn with Qiskit.](figures/rzz-decomposition){#fig-rzz width=45%}

::: {.callout-note}
## Where this returns
@eq-pauli-rotation comes back twice later in the course: in Trotter circuits, where
$e^{-iHt}$ is split into Pauli rotations, and in the parameter-shift rule for gradients.
:::

## Native gate sets {#sec-native-gate-sets}

@tbl-native lists the native gates of some current platforms. Gate names and details
change with each hardware generation; the point is the pattern. Every platform offers
a continuous family of single-qubit rotations and one or two entangling gates.

| Platform | Single-qubit | Two-qubit |
|---|---|---|
| IQM (superconducting) | $\gate{PRX}(\theta,\varphi)$ | CZ |
| IBM (superconducting) | $R_Z$ (virtual), $\sqrt{X}$, $X$ | CZ or ECR |
| Google (superconducting) | PhasedXZ | CZ, $\sqrt{i\mathrm{SWAP}}$ |
| Quantinuum (trapped ions) | $U_{1q}(\theta,\varphi)$, $R_Z$ | $R_{ZZ}(\theta)$, any angle |
| IonQ (trapped ions) | GPi, GPi2 | Mølmer-Sørensen |

: Native gates of some current devices. `TODO` verify against current device specifications. {#tbl-native}

The IQM gate is a rotation about an axis in the $xy$-plane of the Bloch sphere,
$$
\gate{PRX}(\theta,\varphi) = \exp\!\left[-i\frac{\theta}{2}\left(\cos\varphi\, X + \sin\varphi\, Y\right)\right].
$$ {#eq-prx}
The operator in brackets squares to the identity, so @prp-pauli-rotation applies to
it too.

### Why $R_Z$ is free {#sec-virtual-z}

On superconducting devices, $R_Z$ is usually a [virtual Z gate]{.gloss key="virtual-z"}:
no pulse is applied at all. The reason is the conjugation identity
$$
R_Z(\alpha)\, \gate{PRX}(\theta,\varphi)\, R_Z(\alpha)^\dagger = \gate{PRX}(\theta,\varphi+\alpha),
$$ {#eq-virtual-z}
which follows from $R_Z(\alpha) X R_Z(\alpha)^\dagger = \cos\alpha\, X + \sin\alpha\, Y$.
Using @eq-virtual-z, every $R_Z$ can be moved later through the circuit, changing the
phases $\varphi$ of the drive pulses it passes. CZ commutes with $R_Z$, so nothing else
changes. At the end, an $R_Z$ right before a measurement in the computational basis has
no effect and can be dropped.

## Connectivity {#sec-connectivity}

A native two-qubit gate is available only between qubits that are physically coupled.
The [coupling graph]{.gloss key="coupling-graph"} records which pairs these are. On a
superconducting chip it is fixed by fabrication: a square lattice, IBM's heavy-hex
lattice, or IQM's star layout around a central resonator. In a trapped-ion chain all
pairs can interact, at the price of slower gates.

A two-qubit gate between qubits that are not neighbours needs SWAP gates to bring them
together, and each SWAP costs three CNOTs (@fig-swap).

![SWAP as three CNOTs with alternating control.](figures/swap-three-cnots){#fig-swap width=45%}

In practice we do not insert SWAPs by hand: [transpilation]{.gloss key="transpilation"}
maps a circuit onto the native gates and coupling graph of a device. We return to its
cost with the algorithms; for now, remember that connectivity turns into extra
two-qubit gates, and two-qubit gates are the main source of error [@preskill2018].

::: {#exr-swap}
